source: Olausson, Inala, Wang, Gao, Solar-Lezama (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation? (ICLR)
finding: Direct matched-budget test of repair versus plain resampling, with unit tests running. Gains from repair are modest, uneven, and sometimes absent once repair calls are counted.
numbers: HumanEval and APPS (300 APPS tasks: 180 interview, 60 competition, 60 intro). Models: Code Llama-13b, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. Budget = np + np*nfr samples vs i.i.d. baseline of the same size; also pass@t by tokens. GPT-4 on APPS beats baseline by up to 8%; GPT-3.5 on competition problems up to 34% relative gain; GPT-3.5 and Code Llama on APPS mostly match or lag baseline. One cell: 1 initial sample + 10 repairs gave 1.05x pass@20 baseline; 2 initial + 10 repairs each (22 samples) gave 0.97x baseline pass@22.
quote: whether you would--at an equivalent compute budget--have had a greater chance of success if you had simply drawn more code samples
limits: Feedback is written by the same model; tests are given. Older models (2023 endpoints gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, gpt-4-0314). Code only. Not a test of a code-triggered pass versus best-of-N plus a selector, but it is the closest matched-budget comparison found.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 1 only in part. At equal calls, repair is not a clear win over resampling; its edge is largest for the strongest model on the hardest items and when starting samples are diverse. Our S5 must be compared with best-of-N at equal tokens on our own benchmarks.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) feedback-quality experiments (same paper, Sections 4.2 and 4.3)
finding: The bottleneck in repair is the feedback text. A stronger model's feedback makes repair beat both the baseline and plain self-repair at all budgets. Human feedback beats GPT-4's own feedback.
numbers: Boosted feedback (GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 feedback for Code Llama; GPT-4 feedback for GPT-3.5) beat baseline and self-repair at all budgets on APPS. Human study: 16 participants, 2 feedback texts per program. Repair success with GPT-4 feedback 33.30% overall (intro 42.64, interview 19.33, competition 3.67) vs human feedback 52.60% (62.21, 45.67, 14.67). Factor 1.58x.
quote: replacing GPT-4's own explanations with those of a human programmer improves repair significantly
limits: Small human study; time cost of humans not tracked. Code only.
agent_relevance: Answers part of gap 9: for code, a stronger or different feedback source beats self-feedback; human beats model. For open tasks with no tests this is still untested.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: At matched generation budget on MATH, N sequential revisions from a revision-trained model slightly beat N parallel samples, with either a learned verifier or majority vote to choose. The best mix of sequential and parallel depends on difficulty.
numbers: PaLM 2-S* fine-tuned for revision, MATH. Figure 6 right: sequential narrowly outperforms parallel under both selectors. Easy questions do best with purely sequential; hard questions need a balance. Compute-optimal allocation beats parallel best-of-N using up to 4x less test-time compute.
limits: Revision model was fine-tuned for revising (footnote: capability-specific fine-tuning is needed). Verifier is a trained outcome reward model, not a program. Old model family. Does not test a prompt-only revise step.
agent_relevance: Supports a hybrid: spend a few calls on revising, the rest on parallel samples, and choose the mix by item difficulty. Does not show a prompted S5 pass beats best-of-N for frontier models.

source: Snell et al. (2024) revision model overturns correct answers (same paper, Section 6.1)
finding: Even a model trained to revise turns many right answers wrong, so the authors add a selection step over the revision chain.
numbers: Around 38% of correct answers get converted back to incorrect ones with the naive revision approach. Fix: sequential majority vote or verifier-based choice across the chain.
quote: around 38% of correct answers get converted back to incorrect ones
agent_relevance: Bears on gap 4: any revise pass has a cost on already-correct items. Keep the original answer in the pool and let a code check or vote pick, rather than trusting the last revision.

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey (TACL)
finding: Survey of the self-correction literature with a fairness checklist. Many positive results use oracle labels or weak initial prompts. Feedback generation is the bottleneck. Works when reliable external feedback exists, or after large-scale fine-tuning, or on tasks where checking is easier than making (decomposable answers).
numbers: Three conclusions: (1) no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs in general tasks under fair settings; (2) works well with reliable external feedback; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Reflexion, RCI and Self-Refine are listed among studies using oracle information or weak prompts. Example of suited task: CoVe-style lists of many answers that can each be checked.
quote: no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs in general tasks
limits: Survey up to late 2024 (v3 Dec 2024). No new experiments, no 2025 reasoning-model data. Authors expect unexplored tasks where intrinsic correction works.
agent_relevance: Gives the boundary for G2: keep S5 on tasks that have a program check or a decomposable answer; treat free-form self-critique as untrusted.

source: Chen, Lin, Scharli, Zhou (2024) Teaching large language models to self-debug, feedback-format ablation (Table 2)
finding: A bare 'this is wrong' flag, once execution gives it, recovers most of the gain from richer feedback. Adding unit-test text or a trace adds a little. On Spider, with no tests, the bare flag does almost nothing.
numbers: MBPP, GPT-4: baseline 72.8, Simple 78.8, UT 80.6, UT+Expl 80.4, UT+Trace 80.2. GPT-3.5: 67.6, 70.8, 72.2, 74.2, 72.8 (row labels in the extracted table are shifted; order follows the paper text, so treat the GPT-3.5 split as approximate). TransCoder GPT-4: 77.3, 80.9, 88.8, 90.4, 89.5. Spider GPT-4 baseline 73.2, Simple 73.4, +Expl 73.6.
limits: Simple feedback here already uses the execution result when tests exist. Table text extraction was scrambled, so the per-column mapping of UT versus Expl is reconstructed. Few-shot prompts differ in length between formats (6 vs 3 exemplars).
agent_relevance: Bears on gap 3: the failure flag carries the larger share of the gain in code; written explanation adds a small, task-dependent increment.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Self-Debugging without unit-test execution (Table 3)
finding: Without execution, self-debugging gives small gains and can hurt. Models are overconfident in their first code.
numbers: MBPP: Codex 61.4 baseline, Simple 57.6 (down), +Trace 66.2; GPT-3.5 67.6 to 69.2; GPT-4 72.8 to 76.0 to 76.4. TransCoder GPT-3.5 89.1 unchanged in every format; GPT-4 77.3 to 78.4. Text: GPT-4 improves MBPP by 3.6 points, other tasks up to about 1.
limits: Old models (Codex, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 of 2023). One run per cell.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: the execution signal is where most of the lift comes from. Trace-style feedback written by the model is the only self-made signal that consistently helped.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion, Rust-50 ablation (Table 3), re-read this session
finding: On the 50 hardest HumanEval Rust problems, running tests and compiler errors without a written reflection gave no gain over the base model. Adding the written reflection gave +8. So the reflection text did matter here.
numbers: GPT-4 on HumanEval Rust-50. Base 0.60. Without test generation 0.52. Without self-reflection (tests kept) 0.60. Full Reflexion 0.68. Sample is 50 problems, so +8 is 4 problems.
quote: the compromised agent does not improve performance over the baseline run
limits: Correction to the earlier gap wording: Rust-50 does NOT show no change from the lesson. It shows the tests-only arm equals the base, and the lesson adds 0.08. Tiny N, one model.
agent_relevance: Partly closes gap 3. In Reflexion's own data the lesson added 8 points in two places (Rust-50 and HotPotQA). The contrary evidence is Self-Debug (flag gets most of the gain) and Renze (Retry 0.827 vs Explanation 0.876 on failed items). Net: the flag is the larger part, the written lesson adds a few points.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion, HotPotQA episodic-memory ablation
finding: With ground-truth context, keeping the last trajectory (episodic memory) helps, and adding the written self-reflection gives a further 8 points absolute.
numbers: HotPotQA, 100 questions, CoT(GT) baseline, EPM, EPM plus reflection: reflection adds 8% absolute over EPM (Figure 4c).
limits: 100 questions, one model, no confidence interval. Paper calls this support for reflection-guided refinement.
agent_relevance: Same as d08: the written lesson helps by about 8 points in two small tests, but retry-with-flag is the baseline to beat.

source: Tsui (2025, revised Aug 2026 v3) Self-Correction Bench: the self-correction blind spot
finding: Version 3 now includes reasoning models and two Claude models. Reasoning models show a small or even negative blind spot. Non-reasoning models fix an error shown as the user's but miss the same error as their own. Appending 'Wait' removes most of the gap without training.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: 64.5% blind spot; 'Wait' cut it by 89.3% and raised mean accuracy by 156%; fine-tuning on 5,306 traces cut it 76.0%. Claude 3.5 Haiku blind spot 52.5%, Claude Sonnet 4 41.4% (footnote, via prefill). Table 3 mean accuracy, non-reasoning base / with Wait / reasoning sibling: DeepSeek-V3-0324 0.567 / 0.902 / R1-0528 0.908; phi-4 0.325 / 0.701 / reasoning-plus 0.707; Qwen3-14B 0.117 / 0.868 / thinking 0.843; Qwen3-32B 0.045 / 0.793 / 0.894; Qwen3-235B 0.328 / 0.856 / 0.876. R1-Distill-Llama-8B blind spot: SCLI5 49.0%, GSM8K-SC 13.4%; 70B: 11.3% and -3.1%.
quote: reasoning models show a small, even negative, Self-Correction Blind Spot
limits: Read only to character 100000 of 134709. Errors are injected or collected, not an open revise task. 'Wait' needs prefill of the assistant turn, which most closed models do not allow. The 'But' and 'However' figures are in a table not read. Blind spot is about correcting a shown error, not about finding one.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6 for open models and gives two Claude points. Appending 'Wait' as a continuation marker is a free, no-extra-call O8 wording and brings non-reasoning models close to their reasoning siblings. For reasoning models the blind spot is already small, so 'Wait' adds little there.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: simple test-time scaling, budget forcing ablation (Table 4)
finding: Forcing the model to keep thinking by appending 'Wait' scales accuracy on AIME24; other continuation strings or none do less. Gains plateau and the method needs control of the decoding loop.
numbers: s1-32B, trained on 1,000 examples. Extrapolation x2: no string 50.0 AIME24 / 90.2 MATH500 / 55.1 GPQA; 'Alternatively' 50.0 / 92.2 / 59.6; 'Hmm' 50.0 / 93.0 / 59.6; 'Wait' 53.3 / 93.0 / 59.6. No extrapolation 50.0 / 93.0 / 57.6. AIME24 with 'Wait' 1x/2x/4x: 30.0 / 33.3 / 36.7 for s1.
limits: Tokens are not free: forcing adds thinking tokens (cost is in length, not calls). 30 AIME questions, so a 3.3-point gap is one question. One fine-tuned model.
agent_relevance: Supports a neutral continuation marker in O8 for models with an exposed thinking channel. For API models without prefill, the same effect has to come from instruction text, which is untested.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Understanding the dark side of LLMs' intrinsic self-correction (v2, Jul 2025)
finding: Gap 2 evidence. Intrinsic self-correction (no oracle, refine whether right or wrong) lowers accuracy in all four tasks, including for o1-family models. Newer models overturn fewer correct answers on yes/no and reasoning, but not on decision-making. Failure patterns look like human overthinking and perfectionism.
numbers: Models: ChatGPT (o1, o1-preview, o1-mini, 4o, 3.5-turbo), Llama 2/3/3.1, DeepSeek V3 and R1. Tasks: Yes/No QA, HotPotQA (100), HumanEval (161), decision making. Llama-3.1-8B: -20.4 accuracy with 58.8% of correct answers overturned. GPT-3.5-turbo changed 81.3% of answers more than 6 times in 10 samples. o1-mini in decision-making: 15.4 'think' steps in failed cases vs 5.3 in normal cases.
limits: Table columns were scrambled by text extraction, so per-model drops for o1 are not quoted. Prompts remove 'you were unsuccessful' so the model is told nothing. Small sets. No thinking-budget control is varied.
agent_relevance: Partly closes gap 2: for 2024-2025 reasoning models (o1 family, R1) a blind 'are you sure' pass still lowers accuracy. Keep G1/G2: revise only on an outside trigger. Note Tsui finds the blind spot small for reasoning models, so the harm is about unneeded revision, not inability to fix.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) ProcessBench: identifying process errors in mathematical reasoning (abstract)
finding: Locating the earliest wrong step is hard even for strong models. Prompted critic models beat existing process reward models on harder problems. A reasoning model (o1-mini) beats the best open critic (QwQ-32B-Preview), which matches GPT-4o.
numbers: 3,400 test cases, mostly competition and Olympiad level, expert-marked error step. Abstract gives no scores.
limits: Abstract only; scores not read. Model-made locators, not program-made.
agent_relevance: For gap 4: where there is no program check, a reasoning model is the best available locator, but locating is the hard step (Tyen: best model finds first error 52.87% of the time). A program locator, when available, should be preferred.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive behaviors that enable self-improving reasoners (abstract)
finding: Verification and backtracking are among four behaviors that decide whether a base model can profit from RL on verifiable tasks. Models primed with the behaviours improve; the behaviour matters more than whether the priming solutions are correct.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-3B vs Llama-3.2-3B on Countdown. Four behaviours: verification, backtracking, subgoal setting, backward chaining. No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only; training study, not prompt-only.
agent_relevance: Training-side support for keeping verification and backtrack steps in the schema. Not a test of a prompted revise pass.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM evaluators recognize and favor their own generations (abstract)
finding: Models rate their own outputs higher than humans do, and the bias grows with how well they recognise their own text. So a same-model critic is biased.
numbers: GPT-4 and Llama 2 tell their own text from others' above chance. After fine-tuning, self-recognition and self-preference correlate linearly. No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Tested on summarisation-style ratings, not revise loops.
agent_relevance: For gap 9: supports using a different model or a different prompt role as the critic for open tasks. Combined with Tsui (attributing the error to someone else), a different-author framing is the cheapest test.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) survey, open-ended tasks note (Sections 4 and Limitations)
finding: Self-Refine's strong results come from tasks like a constraint sentence (five given words) where checking is easy. The survey says unexplored tasks may exist where intrinsic correction works, and that model-based feedback is available for open-ended text such as dialogue and summaries.
numbers: No new numbers. Notes that model-based evaluators (Fu 2024, Liu 2023) are studied for open text.
limits: Statement of expectation, not a measurement.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open: no measurement of feedback source on open design-like tasks was found. Use a rubric program or a second prompt, and test it on our own tasks.

source: Schon and Wiggins (1992) Kinds of seeing and their functions in designing (Design Studies 13(2)); bibliographic records
finding: Only the Crossref record was opened, not the paper. A sister 1992 record (Kinds of Seeing in Designing) says the case is a workshop example from a first-year design project, told as an illustration of a reflective conversation with the materials. No counts of back-talk events appear in what was seen.
limits: Paper paywalled and not read. The Quist and Petra case in Schon (1983) is a single narrated case, not tallied. I found no source that counts back-talk events in Schon's cases.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open: the only measured human rate of unexpected discoveries remains Suwa 2001 (171 of 606, one architect).

source: Crossref records for Suwa, Gero, Purcell (2000) and Bilda, Gero, Purcell (2006) To sketch or not to sketch?
finding: Records only. Suwa 2000 has 222 citations and Bilda 2006 has 152; both are from the same group. Neither full text was reachable (403 and redirect page). I found no independent group that repeated the unexpected-discovery coding with several designers.
numbers: Crossref cited-by: 222 and 152. No abstract returned. Suwa 2000 per earlier search summary: 173 discoveries of 608 perceptual actions (28.5%), one architect.
limits: Full texts not read. The absence of a replication rests on a failed search (OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar rate-limited, WebSearch budget exhausted), so it is weak.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. Treat the 28% figure as one-expert data and do not use it as a target rate for the agent.
